question: How to manage thrips and leaf curl virus in chilli during vegetative and flowering stages?
answer: Chilli leaf curl is primarily caused by Begomovirus transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), and curling is aggravated by thrips (Scirtothrips dorsalis). IPM protocol: 1. Install 15-20 yellow and blue sticky traps per acre to monitor and reduce vector populations. 2. During early vegetative stage, spray Azadirachtin (Neem oil 10,000 ppm) @ 2 ml/L. 3. If thrips cross Economic Threshold Level (ETL of 2 thrips/leaf), apply Fipronil 5% SC @ 2 ml/L or Spinosad 45% SC @ 0.3 ml/L. Strictly avoid broad-spectrum organophosphates during flowering to protect honeybee pollinators.
source: ICAR-IIHR Package of Practices for Chilli
document_title: ICAR-IIHR Package of Practices for Chilli

question: What is the recommended fertilizer schedule and NPK dosage for chilli in black soil?
answer: For high-yielding chilli in black soil, recommended N:P:K ratio is 120:60:60 kg/acre. Basal application: Apply 10 tonnes FYM/Compost, full dose of Phosphorus (Single Super Phosphate @ 150 kg/acre), 50% Potash (MOP @ 50 kg/acre), and 25% Nitrogen (Urea @ 25 kg/acre) along with Zinc Sulphate @ 10 kg/acre before transplanting. Top dressing: Split the remaining 75% Nitrogen and 50% Potash in three equal splits at 30, 60, and 90 days after transplanting (DAT). Drip fertigation with 19:19:19 water-soluble fertilizer @ 3 kg/acre/week is ideal from vegetative to fruit development.
source: Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University (ANGRAU)
document_title: ANGRAU Chilli Nutrient Management Guidelines

question: How to control chilli anthracnose, dieback, and fruit rot (Colletotrichum capsici)?
answer: Chilli anthracnose causes circular sunken water-soaked spots on ripe fruits and twig die-back from tip downwards. Management: 1. Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride @ 10 g/kg seed or Thiram @ 2.5 g/kg. 2. Remove and burn diseased fruits and twigs. 3. At first sign of foliar spotting, spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L. Repeat at 12-14 day intervals if humid rainy conditions persist. Observe pre-harvest interval (PHI) of 5 days.
source: Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine & Storage (DPPQS)
document_title: DPPQS Major Crop Disease Advisories - Chilli

question: What causes chilli leaves to curl downwards and how to differentiate from thrips?
answer: Downward curling (inverted cup shape) with thickening, brittle texture, and elongated petioles is caused by Yellow Mites (Polyphagotarsonemus latus). In contrast, thrips cause upward boat-shaped leaf cupping with silvery feeding scars along midribs. Mite Management: 1. Avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes succulent foliage. 2. Spray wettable sulphur 80% WDG @ 3 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1 ml/L directed to leaf undersides. 3. Spray organic neem formulation (Azadirachtin 10,000 ppm @ 2 ml/L) during early vegetative stages.
source: ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI)
document_title: IARI Compendium of Vegetable Pests

question: Can moisture stress or water deficit cause chilli leaves to curl?
answer: Yes. Physiological moisture stress causes chilli leaves to roll inward or upward as a protective mechanism to reduce transpiration surface area under high vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and soil moisture tension below -45 kPa (< 40% Available Water Capacity). Unlike virus infection, moisture-stressed leaves do not display mosaic mottling, vein clearing, or severe stunting, and recover turgidity within 6-12 hours after drip irrigation. Remediation: Irrigate when root-zone soil moisture drops to 50% AWC; apply organic paddy straw mulch to conserve moisture.
source: ICAR-Central Institute for Arid Horticulture (CIAH)
document_title: CIAH Crop Water Stress & Irrigation Guidelines

question: When should I irrigate my chilli crop and what are the critical growth stages?
answer: Chilli requires 600-800 mm water across its 150-180 day cycle. Critical stages where moisture deficit causes severe yield loss: 1. Establishment / Transplanting stage (days 1-15): Light daily watering. 2. Vegetative branching (days 25-45): Irrigate at -35 kPa soil tension (50-60% AWC). 3. Flowering and fruit set (days 50-85): Most critical; moisture stress causes heavy flower and fruit drop, while excess waterlogging induces root rot. 4. Fruit ripening / picking: Moderate irrigation to avoid fruit splitting. Drip irrigation at 2.5-3.5 mm/day is optimal.
source: ANGRAU Water Technology Centre
document_title: ANGRAU Water Management Protocols for Commercial Crops

question: How to control bacterial leaf spot (Xanthomonas campestris) in chilli?
answer: Bacterial leaf spot causes dark, water-soaked circular lesions with yellow halos on leaves, leading to severe defoliation during warm rainy weather. Management: 1. Treat seed with Hot water (50°C for 25 min) or Streptocycline @ 100 ppm for 30 min. 2. Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L + Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L (1 g/10L water) at first onset of spots. Repeat after 12 days if rainy humid conditions persist. 3. Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation to stop bacterial splash dissemination.
source: ICAR-IIHR Package of Practices for Chilli
document_title: ICAR-IIHR Package of Practices for Chilli

question: What is the cost of cultivation, expected yield, and profit economics for 1 acre of dry red chilli?
answer: Economic benchmarks for dry red chilli cultivation (Guntur/Andhra Pradesh benchmark): 1. Total Cost of Cultivation: ₹92,000 - ₹98,000 per acre (including land prep, seed/nursery, drip/mulch, fertilizer, crop protection, and picking labor). 2. Expected Yield: 22 to 26 quintals per acre of cured dry pods under drip fertigation and IPM. 3. Gross Realization: At modal price of ₹10,500/quintal, gross revenue is ₹2,31,000 - ₹2,73,000. 4. Net Profit: ₹1,35,000 - ₹1,75,000 per acre over a 6-month crop cycle.
source: ICAR-IIHR & ANGRAU Agricultural Economics Survey
document_title: ANGRAU Farm Enterprise Cost & Return Studies

question: What are the maturity indices and post-harvest drying standards for red chilli?
answer: Harvest chilli pods when they turn deep, uniform dark red. Pick in 3-4 pickings to maximize grade quality. Post-harvest drying: 1. Harvested pods must be dried immediately from ~70% moisture down to 10-11% safe storage moisture. 2. Dry on clean cement threshing floors or polythene tarpaulins; avoid bare soil contact to prevent aflatoxin contamination. 3. Turn pods 2-3 times daily for uniform drying; cover during nights to avoid dew condensation. Properly dried chillies rattle when shaken.
source: Spices Board of India (Ministry of Commerce)
document_title: Spices Board Good Post-Harvest Practices for Chilli

question: How to control early blight and late blight in tomato plants?
answer: Tomato Early Blight (Alternaria solani) exhibits concentric target-board rings on lower leaves, while Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans) shows dark water-soaked greasy lesions during cool, misty weather. Protocol: 1. Prune lower diseased foliage up to 20 cm from ground level to improve aeration and prevent splash dispersal. 2. For early blight: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2 g/L. 3. For late blight outbreaks: Apply systemic Metalaxyl-M 4% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2 g/L. Use drip irrigation and strictly avoid evening overhead sprinkler wetting of foliage.
disease: Alternaria solani (Early Blight), Phytophthora infestans (Late Blight)
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR)
document_title: ICAR-IIVR Tomato Pathology Guidelines

question: How to manage Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) and whitefly vector?
answer: Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) causes upward cupping, severe leaf wrinkling, chlorosis, and dwarfed bushy growth. Management focuses on whitefly vector control: 1. Install 15-20 yellow sticky traps per acre at canopy height. 2. Mulch planting beds with silver reflective polyethylene film to repel alighting whiteflies. 3. Nursery net cover (40-mesh nylon) to raise virus-free seedlings. 4. Field spray Azadirachtin (Neem oil 10,000 ppm) @ 2 ml/L or Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.3 ml/L during vegetative stage. Rogue out and bury severely stunted infected plants early.
source: ICAR Package of Practices for Solanaceous Vegetables
document_title: ICAR Package of Practices for Solanaceous Vegetables

question: What should I do if my tomato leaves have brown spots?
answer: Brown spots on tomato foliage typically indicate fungal leaf spots: 1. Early Blight (Alternaria solani): Brown spots with prominent concentric rings on older lower leaves. Prune infected leaves and spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Azoxystrobin @ 1 ml/L. 2. Septoria Leaf Spot: Small, circular brown spots with gray centers and black specks. Spray Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2 g/L. 3. Bacterial Spot: Small dark brown water-soaked lesions. Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L. Action: Send a close-up photo of the leaf spot via the camera button for AI visual confirmation before applying chemical sprays.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR)
document_title: IIVR Diagnostic Guide for Foliar Vegetable Diseases

question: What is the recommended fertilizer schedule for tomato and how to prevent Blossom End Rot?
answer: Tomato requires balanced N:P:K of 120:60:120 kg/acre. Basal application: 10 tonnes FYM, full Phosphorus (SSP 150 kg/acre), 25% Nitrogen (Urea 25 kg/acre), and 25% Potash (MOP 25 kg/acre). Top dressing: Split remaining N and K in 3 equal parts at 25, 45, and 65 days after transplanting. Blossom End Rot (black leathery rot at fruit bottom) is caused by Calcium deficiency exacerbated by irregular watering. Prevention: Apply Calcium Nitrate @ 2-3 kg/acre via drip weekly from flowering, or foliar spray Calcium Chloride 0.5% (5 g/L) twice during fruit development.
source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) Agritech Portal
document_title: TNAU Crop Production Guide - Vegetables

question: How much profit can I get from one acre of tomato cultivation and what are the costs?
answer: Tomato economics per acre (ICAR-IIVR and SAU benchmarks): 1. Total Cultivation Cost: ₹65,000 - ₹72,000 per acre (hybrid seeds, staking, drip system, fertilizers, labor, harvesting). 2. Expected Yield: 250 to 300 quintals (25-30 tonnes) per acre under good management with hybrid cultivars. 3. Gross Returns: At average farm-gate modal price of ₹1,200/quintal (₹12/kg), gross realization is ₹3,00,000 - ₹3,60,000. 4. Net Profit: ₹2,20,000 - ₹2,80,000 per acre over 120-140 days. Note: Tomato prices fluctuate significantly; seasonal price crashes to ₹400/quintal reduce net returns to ₹35,000/acre.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR)
document_title: IIVR Technical Bulletin on Vegetable Enterprise Economics

question: What is the IPM strategy for pink bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella) in cotton?
answer: Pink bollworm attacks squaring, flowering, and boll development stages, causing rosette flowers and premature boll opening. Management: 1. Install 5 pheromone traps (Pectino-lure) per acre for monitoring. ETL is 8 moths/trap/night for 3 consecutive days or 10% damaged green bolls/rosetted flowers. 2. At ETL, spray Neem formulation Azadirachtin 1500 ppm @ 5 ml/L. 3. If infestation persists, apply Emamectin Benzoate 5% SG @ 4.4 g/10L or Chlorpyrifos 20% EC @ 2.5 ml/L (on non-food field crop). 4. Terminate crop by mid-January to break pest lifecycle; strictly avoid ratooning.
source: ICAR-Central Institute for Cotton Research (CICR), Nagpur
document_title: CICR Pink Bollworm Management Protocols

question: How to control sucking pests (jassids, aphids, whiteflies) in Bt cotton?
answer: Early season sucking pests cause leaf curling, yellowing of margins, and hopper burn. IPM: 1. Seed treatment with Imidacloprid 70% WS @ 5 g/kg seed. 2. Install 15 yellow sticky traps per acre for whiteflies and aphids. 3. Conserve ladybird beetles and chrysoperla predators. 4. If leaf hopper population crosses ETL (2 hoppers/leaf): Spray Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Dinotefuran 20% SG @ 0.3 g/L. Avoid synthetic pyrethroids which trigger secondary whitefly and mite resurgence.
pest: Amrasca biguttula (Jassid), Aphis gossypii, Bemisia tabaci
source: Professor Jayashankar Telangana State Agricultural University (PJTSAU)
document_title: PJTSAU Commercial Crop IPM Manual

question: How to control bacterial leaf blight and blast in paddy/rice?
answer: For Rice Blast (Magnaporthe oryzae) with diamond/spindle-shaped lesions: Drain excess water, avoid excessive urea application, and spray Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 0.6 g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 1.5 ml/L. For Bacterial Leaf Blight (Xanthomonas oryzae) with wavy yellow straw margins: Drain field, delay nitrogen top-dressing, and apply Copper Hydroxide 53.8% DF @ 2 g/L. Note: Farmer-facing automated chemical recommendations for rice remain in RESEARCH_ONLY validation status; consult local KVK officer.
source: ICAR-National Rice Research Institute (NRRI), Cuttack
document_title: NRRI Rice Disease Management Compendium

question: What is Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) irrigation in rice and how does it save water?
answer: Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) is a controlled water management technique where the paddy field is allowed to dry until water drops to 15 cm below soil surface (monitored using a perforated PVC 'pani pipe') before reflooding to 5 cm depth. Benefits: 1. Saves 25-35% irrigation water without reducing grain yield. 2. Reduces methane greenhouse gas emissions by up to 40%. 3. Improves root aeration and reduces lodging. Keep 2-5 cm standing water continuously only during flowering (heading) to ensure pollination.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Rice Research (IIRR), Hyderabad
document_title: IIRR Sustainable Water Management Bulletin

question: How to prevent and manage Late Blight in potato crops?
answer: Potato Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans) develops rapidly in misty weather when relative humidity exceeds 85% and temperature is 10-20°C. Protocol: 1. Preventive spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L as canopy closes. 2. If water-soaked blighted lesions appear: Spray Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2 g/L or Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1 g/L + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L. 3. Ensure high earthing-up to prevent zoospores washing into soil to infect tubers. Observe 7-day pre-harvest interval.
source: ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI), Shimla
document_title: CPRI Potato Pathology & Crop Protection Bulletin

question: How to control Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) in maize / corn?
answer: Fall Armyworm causes skeletonized leaves and windowing in whorls with heavy frass. IPM Protocol: 1. Deep summer ploughing to expose pupae to predatory birds. 2. Install FAW pheromone traps @ 5 per acre. 3. Early vegetative (Whorl stage): Spray bio-pesticide Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) kurstaki @ 2 g/L or Metarhizium anisopliae @ 5 g/L directed into plant whorls. 4. For severe infestation exceeding 10% damaged plants: Apply Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC @ 0.4 ml/L or Spinetoram 11.7% SC @ 0.5 ml/L directed into the central whorl.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Maize Research (IIMR), Ludhiana
document_title: IIMR Fall Armyworm Management Compendium

question: How to control Sigatoka leaf spot and Panama wilt in banana?
answer: Yellow and Black Sigatoka cause necrotic spindle streaks coalescing into leaf blight. Management: 1. Maintain plantation sanitation; prune and burn severely blighted leaves. 2. Improve drainage to reduce microclimate humidity. 3. Foliar spray Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/L mixed with mineral oil (10 ml/L) or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 g/L. For Panama Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum): Drench rhizome root zone with Trichoderma viride enriched FYM @ 5 kg/plant; rotate with lowland flooded paddy where possible.
source: ICAR-National Research Centre for Banana (NRCB), Tiruchirappalli
document_title: NRCB Banana Disease Diagnostic Compendium

question: Which crops are suitable for black cotton soil (Vertisols)?
answer: Black cotton soils (Vertisols) have high montmorillonite clay (> 40%), deep profile, and exceptional moisture-holding capacity. Highly suitable crops: 1. Cash Crops: Cotton, Chilli, Tobacco. 2. Pulses: Chickpea (Bengal gram), Pigeonpea (Red gram), Black gram. 3. Oilseeds: Soybean, Sunflower, Safflower. 4. Cereals: Sorghum (Jowar), Post-rainy Rabi Wheat, Maize. Management caution: High clay causes slow internal drainage; in high rainfall zones, adopt Broad-Bed and Furrow (BBF) or Ridge-and-Furrow systems to prevent waterlogging and root asphyxiation.
keywords: which crop is suitable for black soil
source: National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP)
document_title: NBSS&LUP Soil Resource Mapping & Crop Suitability Guide

question: What are the properties and management of red sandy loam soils (Alfisols)?
answer: Red sandy loam soils (Alfisols) are shallow to medium in depth, light-textured, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0-7.2), with fast infiltration and low moisture-holding capacity. Suitable crops: Groundnut, Pigeonpea, Tomato, Finger Millet (Ragi), Castor, and Maize. Management: 1. Incorporate 10-15 tonnes FYM or compost per acre to enhance water retention. 2. Practice frequent light irrigations via drip or furrow. 3. Apply mulching to arrest evaporative losses. 4. Correct low phosphorus with Single Super Phosphate.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Soil Science (IISS), Bhopal
document_title: IISS Soil Management Bulletins

question: What is crop rotation and why is it recommended after chilli or cotton?
answer: Crop rotation is the practice of planting different crop families sequentially in the same field across seasons. Benefits: 1. Nitrogen fixation: Following solanaceous (chilli) or malvaceous (cotton) heavy feeders with legumes (chickpea, black gram, green gram, groundnut) enriches soil nitrogen by 20-40 kg/ha via Rhizobium root nodules. 2. Pest cycle disruption: Breaking the host plant sequence reduces soil-borne inoculum (such as Fusarium and root-knot nematodes) by 30-50%. 3. Improved soil structure and organic carbon.
source: ICAR Handbook of Agriculture (7th Edition)
document_title: ICAR Handbook of Agriculture

question: What are the benefits of drip irrigation and how does it save water?
answer: Drip (micro-irrigation) delivers water and soluble nutrients directly to the plant root zone through emitters under low pressure. Key advantages: 1. Water savings: Reduces irrigation water requirement by 40% to 60% compared to flood/furrow irrigation by eliminating evaporation and deep percolation losses. 2. Water Use Efficiency (WUE): Reaches 90% or higher. 3. Fertigation precision: Nutrients are applied in synchrony with crop uptake, reducing fertilizer leaching and saving 25-30% fertilizer. 4. Reduced weed growth between crop rows.
source: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) - Guidelines
document_title: PMKSY Technical Guidelines on Micro-Irrigation

question: What causes yellow leaves (chlorosis) in crops and how to treat it?
answer: Yellow leaves (chlorosis) are caused by nutritional deficiencies or waterlogging: 1. Nitrogen deficiency: Lower older leaves turn pale yellow uniformly from tip along midrib while upper leaves remain green. Remedy: Soil top-dressing of Urea or foliar spray of 1-2% Urea (10-20 g/L). 2. Iron deficiency: Youngest top leaves turn pale yellow/ivory white with green veins (interveinal chlorosis). Remedy: Foliar spray of Ferrous Sulphate @ 5 g/L + Citric acid @ 1 g/L. 3. Zinc deficiency: Bronzing and yellowish mottling on middle leaves. Remedy: Zinc Sulphate 0.5% (5 g/L) foliar spray. 4. Root waterlogging: Ensure drainage channels are clear.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Soil Science (IISS), Bhopal
document_title: IISS Diagnostic Key for Plant Nutrient Deficiencies

question: What is Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and its core steps?
answer: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is an ecologically sound, comprehensive pest management strategy combining cultural, mechanical, biological, and chemical tools to keep pest populations below the Economic Threshold Level (ETL). Core steps: 1. Cultural controls: Crop rotation, resistant crop varieties, summer ploughing, optimal spacing. 2. Mechanical controls: Hand-picking caterpillars, 15-20 yellow/blue sticky traps and pheromone traps per acre. 3. Biological controls: Parasitoids (Trichogramma), predators (ladybird beetles), and entomopathogens (Beauveria, Metarhizium). 4. Chemical controls: Strictly as a targeted last resort using selective green/blue triangle pesticides with PPE.
source: National Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM), New Delhi
document_title: NCIPM Principles of Integrated Pest Management

question: What are the weather safety rules and best conditions for spraying agrochemicals?
answer: Spraying agrochemicals requires strict alignment with atmospheric conditions: 1. Rain Safety: Do not spray if forecast rainfall probability exceeds 35% within 6 hours, as rain washes active ingredients into non-target soil. 2. Wind Limits: Optimal wind speed is 3 to 15 km/h. Wind > 15 km/h causes severe spray drift; wind < 2.5 km/h with temperature > 32°C causes thermal inversion and chemical vapor lock. 3. Temperature Window: Spray during early morning (6:00 - 9:00 AM) or late afternoon (4:30 - 6:30 PM). 4. Mandatory Safety Gear: Wear chemical-resistant gloves, face mask, eye goggles, and full-length clothing. Never spray against wind direction.
source: Central Insecticides Board & Registration Committee (CIBRC)
document_title: CIBRC Guidelines on Safe Agrochemical Application

question: How much fertilizer should I apply if crop and soil are not specified?
answer: Fertilizer dosage cannot be prescribed without knowing the specific crop, growth stage, soil type, and existing soil nutrient status (from a Soil Health Card). General principles: 1. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth, Phosphorus promotes root development, and Potassium enhances fruit quality and pest resistance. 2. Applying indiscriminate high doses of Nitrogen (Urea) causes succulent growth vulnerable to thrips, sucking pests, and fungal blight. Always specify your crop and growth stage, or consult your latest Soil Health Card test report before applying chemical fertilizers.
source: Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DA&FW)
document_title: National Soil Health & Balanced Fertilization Guidelines

question: What is the PM-KISAN scheme, eligibility criteria, and payment schedule?
answer: Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) is a Central Sector Scheme providing income support of ₹6,000 per year to all landholding farmer families across India. The benefit is disbursed directly to aadhaar-linked bank accounts in three equal 4-monthly installments of ₹2,000 each (April-July, August-November, December-March). Eligibility: All cultivable landholding farmer families. Exclusions: Institutional landholders, serving/retired government employees, income tax payees, and constitutional post holders. Mandatory requirement: e-KYC on the pmkisan.gov.in portal.
source: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India
document_title: PM-KISAN Operational Guidelines

question: What is PMFBY crop insurance and how can farmers claim compensation for crop loss?
answer: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) provides comprehensive crop insurance coverage against non-preventable natural risks from pre-sowing to post-harvest. Premium rates paid by farmers: Kharif food and oilseed crops: 2%, Rabi food and oilseeds: 1.5%, Annual Commercial and Horticultural crops (Chilli, Tomato, Cotton): 5%. Claim Protocol for localized calamities (hailstorm, landslide, inundation, cyclone): The farmer must notify the insurance company, bank, or agricultural department within 72 hours of the event via the Crop Insurance App or toll-free number 1800-180-1551.
source: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare - PMFBY Directorate
document_title: PMFBY Revised Operational Guidelines

question: What subsidy is available for installing drip irrigation under PMKSY Per Drop More Crop?
answer: Under the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) - Per Drop More Crop (PDMC), capital subsidy is provided to farmers installing drip and sprinkler systems: 1. Small and Marginal Farmers (landholding up to 2 hectares / 5 acres): 55% financial assistance on system cost. 2. Other Farmers: 45% financial assistance. In states like Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, state supplementary top-up provides up to 70-90% subsidy for SC/ST and small farmers. Application requires land passbook (1B/Patta), Aadhaar card, soil/water test report, and bank passbook through the state micro-irrigation portal (e.g. APMIP).
source: Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, PMKSY-PDMC
document_title: PMKSY Per Drop More Crop Operational Guidelines

question: How should a farmer decide whether to sell chilli now or hold in cold storage?
answer: Commercial decision framework for selling dry red chilli: 1. Compare Current Mandi Price with Historical Benchmark: If Guntur APMC modal price is above ₹12,500/qtl and arrivals are high, selling immediately captures peak margins without storage risk. 2. Cold Storage Cost Analysis: Cold storage costs ~₹80-100 per bag (40 kg) per month plus loading/insurance (~₹250/qtl/quarter). Only hold stock if the anticipated seasonal price rise in 3-4 months exceeds ₹400-500/quintal. 3. Quality Degradation Risk: Ensure moisture is strictly <= 10% before bagging; high moisture chillies turn black in cold storage and face price deductions.
source: Directorate of Marketing & Inspection (DMI) / AGMARKNET
document_title: AGMARKNET Post-Harvest Marketing Advisories

question: How to control fruit borer caterpillar in tomato?
answer: Tomato Fruit Borer is caused by Helicoverpa armigera. Symptoms: Caterpillars bore circular holes into green and ripening tomato fruits, feeding internally with part of their body outside. Management: 1. Cultural & Mechanical: Plant 1 row of African tall marigold as a trap crop for every 16 rows of tomato; install 5 Helicoverpa pheromone traps per acre for ETL monitoring. 2. Biological: Release Trichogramma chilonis egg parasitoids @ 50,000/acre at flower initiation. Spray HaNPV @ 250 LE/acre with 1% jaggery in evening hours. 3. Chemical: Spray Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC @ 0.3 ml/L or Emamectin Benzoate 5% SG @ 0.5 g/L.
source: ICAR-National Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM)
document_title: NCIPM Tomato IPM Technical Manual

question: How to manage whitefly and Cotton Leaf Curl Disease (CLCuD)?
answer: Cotton Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) damages cotton directly by sucking cell sap and secreting honeydew (causing sooty mold), and acts as the vector for Cotton Leaf Curl Begomovirus (CLCuD). Symptoms of CLCuD: Upward leaf curling, thickening of veins, and formation of leaf-like enations on leaf undersides, severely arresting boll development. Management: 1. Spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.25 g/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.4 g/L or Pyriproxyfen 10% EC @ 2 ml/L. 2. Install 20 yellow sticky traps per acre. 3. Eradicate weed hosts like Abutilon indicum and Xanthium strumarium along farm bunds.
source: ICAR-Central Institute for Cotton Research (CICR), Nagpur
document_title: CICR Advisory on Whitefly & Cotton Leaf Curl Virus

question: How to manage sheath blight disease in paddy / rice?
answer: Rice Sheath Blight is caused by Rhizoctonia solani. Symptoms: Greenish-grey oval or irregular snake-skin lesions on lower leaf sheaths near water level. Lesions enlarge and coalesce with dark brown borders, spreading upward to flag leaves. Management: 1. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer (apply N in 3 split doses). 2. Keep bunds clean of grass weeds. 3. Fungicide spray at first appearance: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1 ml/L or Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 2 ml/L or Validamycin 3% L @ 2.5 ml/L, directing spray towards the base of rice hills.
source: ICAR-National Rice Research Institute (NRRI), Cuttack
document_title: NRRI Rice Disease Identification & Management Guide

question: How to control Brown Planthopper (BPH) and hopper burn in paddy?
answer: Brown Planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens) causes 'hopper burn' where rice plants in circular patches turn yellow, dry out, and lodge as if burnt. Management: 1. Form 'alleyways' or walking paths (skipping one row every 2-3 meters) during transplanting to allow sunlight and aeration to reach hill bases. 2. Drain standing water from the field for 3-4 days to suppress nymph populations. 3. Avoid synthetic pyrethroids which cause BPH resurgence. 4. Chemical spray directed at plant base: Pymetrozine 50% WDG @ 0.6 g/L or Triflumezopyrim 10% SC @ 0.5 ml/L or Dinotefuran 20% SG @ 0.4 g/L.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Rice Research (IIRR), Hyderabad
document_title: IIRR Pest Management Protocols for Rice

question: How to control Tikka leaf spot disease and collar rot in groundnut?
answer: Groundnut Tikka Leaf Spot (Cercospora arachidicola & Phaeoisariopsis personata): Symptoms: Dark brown circular spots surrounded by yellow halos on leaflets, causing premature defoliation. Management: 1. Seed treatment with Mancozeb @ 2g/kg or Trichoderma viride @ 4g/kg seed. 2. Foliar spray at first appearance (30-40 DAS): Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2 g/L. 3. Apply Gypsum @ 400-500 kg/ha at flowering/pegging stage (40-45 DAS) to supply calcium and sulphur for pod filling.
symptoms: circular brown spots on groundnut leaves
source: ICAR-Directorate of Groundnut Research (DGR), Junagadh
document_title: DGR Package of Practices for Groundnut

question: How to manage Yellow Mosaic Virus and stem fly in soybean?
answer: Soybean Yellow Mosaic Virus (YMV) is transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Symptoms: Bright yellow patches intermingled with green areas on young leaves, resulting in complete yellowing and stunting. Management: 1. Grow resistant varieties (e.g. JS 20-34, JS 20-29). 2. Seed treatment with Thiamethoxam 30% FS @ 10 ml/kg seed protects seedlings from whitefly and stem fly for 20-25 days. 3. Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Betacyfluthrin + Imidacloprid @ 0.7 ml/L at first appearance of vector whiteflies.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Soybean Research (IISR), Indore
document_title: IISR Soybean Integrated Pest & Disease Management

question: How to manage rust diseases (yellow, brown, black) in wheat?
answer: Wheat Rusts: 1. Yellow (Stripe) Rust: Pustules form in continuous yellow stripes along leaf veins in cool northern regions. 2. Brown (Leaf) Rust: Orange-brown circular pustules scattered randomly over leaf blades. 3. Black (Stem) Rust: Reddish-brown to black elongated pustules on stems and leaf sheaths. Management: 1. Grow rust-resistant varieties (HD 2967, HD 3086, DBW 187). 2. Spray Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/L (500 ml/ha in 500 L water) at first detection of stripe or leaf rust pustules. Repeat after 15 days if cool humid conditions persist.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Wheat & Barley Research (IIWBR), Karnal
document_title: IIWBR Wheat Crop Protection Bulletin

question: How to reclaim and manage saline and alkaline (usar) soils?
answer: Saline and Alkaline Soil Management: 1. Alkaline / Sodic Soil Reclamation (pH > 8.5, high ESP): Apply Agricultural Gypsum (calcium sulphate) based on soil gypsum requirement (usually 3-5 tonnes/ha for moderate sodicity). Follow with deep ponding of good quality water to leach displaced sodium. 2. Green Manuring: Incorporate Sesbania aculeata (Dhaincha) at 45-50 days before flowering to produce organic acids that lower soil pH. 3. Saline Soils (EC > 4 dS/m, normal pH): Provide sub-surface drainage trenches and leach salts with fresh water; grow salt-tolerant crops like barley, mustard, or cotton.
source: ICAR-Central Soil Salinity Research Institute (CSSRI), Karnal
document_title: CSSRI Guidelines for Reclamation of Salt-Affected Soils

question: How to take soil samples and interpret a Soil Health Card (SHC)?
answer: Soil Sampling & Soil Health Card Protocol: 1. Sampling Procedure: Take 8-10 'V'-shaped core samples (0-15 cm depth for field crops, 0-30 cm for fruit trees) across the field in a zig-zag pattern, avoiding bunds, tree shades, and manure pits. Mix thoroughly, air dry in shade, and retain 500g using quartering method. 2. Key SHC Parameters: pH (optimal: 6.5-7.5), EC (< 1 dS/m safe), Organic Carbon (OC > 0.75% high, < 0.5% low), Available N (< 280 kg/ha low, 280-560 medium), Available P2O5 (< 23 kg/ha low), Available K2O (< 140 kg/ha low). Use SHC dosage recommendations to avoid over-applying Urea.
source: Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare - Soil Health Division
document_title: National Soil Testing & Soil Health Card Manual

question: What are the critical growth stages for irrigating crops to prevent moisture stress?
answer: Critical Crop Irrigation Stages (moisture stress during these stages causes irreversible yield loss): 1. Chilli: Flowering, fruit set, and pod development. 2. Tomato: Transplant establishment, active flowering, and fruit enlargement. 3. Cotton: Square formation, flowering, and boll development (withhold water during boll opening). 4. Rice: Panicle initiation, heading, and flowering. 5. Maize: Tasseling and silking stages. 6. Wheat: Crown Root Initiation (CRI at 21 DAS) and flowering/milking.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Water Management (IIWM), Bhubaneswar
document_title: IIWM Technical Bulletin on Crop Water Scheduling
section: Phenological Critical Stages for Micro & Surface Irrigation

question: How to interpret tensiometer and soil moisture sensor readings for irrigation decisions?
answer: Soil Matric Tension & Available Water Capacity (AWC) Interpretation: 1. 0 to -10 kPa (AWC > 90%): Saturated soil / field capacity. Do NOT irrigate; roots suffer oxygen starvation if prolonged. 2. -10 to -30 kPa (AWC 70-90%): Ideal soil moisture condition. Excellent nutrient and water uptake. 3. -35 to -50 kPa (AWC 35-50%): Management Allowed Depletion (MAD) threshold for solanaceous vegetables (Chilli, Tomato) and sensitive crops. Start drip irrigation now. Soil tension reaching -45 kPa indicates impending moisture stress and foliar wilting/curling. 4. Below -65 kPa: Severe drought stress, stomatal closure, leaf curling, and flower drop.
source: ICAR-IIWM Bhubaneswar
document_title: Precision Irrigation Sensor Calibration & Thresholds
section: Soil Matric Potential & Automated Irrigation Triggers

question: How to protect crops from heat waves and high temperatures?
answer: High Temperature and Heat Wave Management: When maximum temperatures exceed 38-40°C: 1. Irrigation: Provide light and frequent drip irrigations in early morning or evening hours to cool the root microclimate; avoid heavy mid-day watering. 2. Foliar Protection: Spray 1% Potassium Nitrate (KNO3) (10 g/L) or Salicylic Acid (100 ppm) to enhance stomatal regulation and mitigate heat shock. 3. Mulching: Organic straw mulching or silver-black reflective plastic mulch reduces soil temperature by 3-5°C and conserves moisture.
source: India Meteorological Department (IMD) - Agromet Advisory Service / ICAR-CRIDA
document_title: IMD-CRIDA Agro-Meteorological Contingency Guidelines

question: What measures should farmers take before and after heavy rainfall or cyclones?
answer: Excess Rainfall and Cyclone Agronomic Measures: 1. Pre-rain: Clear all main and lateral field drainage channels; harvest mature pods or fruits; withhold foliar sprays and fertilizer applications. 2. Post-rain Drainage: Drain excess standing water within 24-48 hours to avoid root hypoxia and collar rot. 3. Foliar Revival: After water recedes and soil aerates, spray 1% 19:19:19 + 0.5% Zinc Sulphate to revive stunted root activity. 4. Disease Prophylaxis: Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L to check bacterial and fungal soft rots.
source: Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University (ANGRAU) / IMD Amaravati
document_title: ANGRAU Cyclone & Excess Rainfall Contingency Bulletins

question: What is the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme, interest rate, and collateral limits?
answer: Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme: 1. Credit Limit: Revolving cash credit for short-term crop loans, post-harvest expenses, and farm maintenance. Collateral-free loan limit is up to ₹1.60 lakh (extendable to ₹3.00 lakh under tie-up arrangements). 2. Subsidized Interest: Standard interest rate is 7% per annum; the Government of India provides a 3% prompt repayment incentive (PRI), bringing the effective interest rate down to 4% per annum for farmers repaying within 1 year. 3. Application: Apply at any commercial bank, RRB, or Primary Agricultural Cooperative Society (PACS) with land patta and Aadhaar.
source: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) / Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare
document_title: Kisan Credit Card Revised Scheme Guidelines

question: How to control red rot disease in sugarcane and what is the package of practices?
answer: Sugarcane red rot (Colletotrichum falcatum) package of practices: 1. Use certified healthy disease-free seed setts from disease-resistant varieties such as Co 0238, Co 86032, or Co 11015. 2. Sett treatment: Treat two-budded or three-budded setts with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 g/L water or moist hot air treatment (MHAT) at 54°C for 2.5 hours prior to planting. 3. Field sanitation: Rogue out infected clumps immediately along with roots and destroy them by burning. 4. Drainage: Prevent waterlogging and avoid flood irrigation across infected and healthy blocks. 5. Crop rotation: Practice crop rotation with paddy, green manure (dhaincha), or pulses for at least 2 seasons to exhaust soil-borne inoculum.
source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Sugarcane Research (IISR) Lucknow
document_title: Sugarcane Red Rot Package of Practices and Integrated Disease Management

question: What is the apple scab spray schedule and management practices?
answer: Apple scab (Venturia inaequalis) spray schedule and management guidelines: 1. Silver tip stage to Green tip stage: Spray Captan 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 3 g/L. 2. Pink bud stage: Spray Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.3 ml/L or Dodine 65% WP @ 0.75 g/L to protect expanding blossom tissue. 3. Petal fall stage: Spray Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 1 ml/L or Trifloxystrobin 25% + Tebuconazole 50% WG @ 0.4 g/L. 4. Fruit let stage: Apply Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L. 5. Post-harvest orchard sanitation: Spray 5% Urea solution on fallen leaves in autumn to accelerate leaf decomposition and suppress pseudothecia overwintering.
source: Dr. YS Parmar University of Horticulture and Forestry / ICAR-CITH
document_title: Apple Scab Spray Schedule and Integrated Orchard Health Advisory
